entries.meaning: Kaikeyi gave no answer; unbearable anger had hardened her, and she glared like a hungry tigress among deer. Taking her condition as incurable, the women left, calling her witless and ill-fated. Throughout the city men and women lamented and poured countless curses on the author of this intrigue. Tormented as though by a fierce fever, the people saw no hope of life without Rāma; the subjects, distraught at the vast separation, resembled aquatic creatures while their water dries away. Amid this universal grief Rāma went to his mother with a serene face and fourfold eagerness, concealing his concern lest the king detain him. Hearing of the forest journey, Rāma's heart rejoiced like a young elephant that knows it has slipped the royal tether.

The ornament of Raghu's line joined his hands and joyfully bowed his head at his mother's feet. She blessed him, drew him to her breast, and made gifts of ornaments and garments. Again and again she kissed his face; tears of love filled her eyes and her body thrilled. She held him in her lap and then pressed him to her heart while her lovely breasts streamed with the milk of affection. Her love and delight cannot be told: it was as though a pauper had attained Kubera's rank. Gazing respectfully at his beautiful face, his mother sweetly asked when the joyous, auspicious hour would come. The moment everyone longed for as intensely as thirsty chātaka birds await the autumn rain under Svāti would crown the merit, character, happiness, and fulfillment of her life.

Kausalyā urged her son to bathe quickly, eat whatever sweet food pleased him, and then go to his father, for the hour was already late. Her favorable words were flowers on the wish-fulfilling tree of love, filled with the nectar of joy; yet Rāma's bee-like mind did not lose itself in them. Knowing the course of dharma, he gently told her that his father had given him the kingdom of the forest, where important work awaited him. He asked his mother cheerfully to permit his auspicious departure and not, through affection, to fear anything, since her grace would be his joy. He would dwell in the woods for fourteen years, make his father's word true, and return to see her feet again; she should not let her heart grow sad.

Rāma's humble, sweet words struck his mother's heart like arrows. Hearing that outwardly soothing speech, she shrank and withered like a javāsa plant when the monsoon rain falls. Her anguish cannot be described: she seemed a doe hearing a lion's roar. Her eyes filled, her body trembled, and she was like a fish caught in a measuring vessel. Steadying herself and looking at her son's face, the mother spoke with a choking voice: his father loved him as life itself and daily delighted in his conduct, so why, after fixing an auspicious day to give him the kingdom, had he ordered him to the forest, and for what offense? She asked what fire had arisen in the solar dynasty. Seeing Rāma's expression, the minister's son explained the cause; on hearing it she sat mute, in a state beyond description.

Kausalyā could neither keep Rāma back nor tell him to go; either course burned her heart terribly. Fate's crooked movement toward everyone was like beginning to draw the moon but finishing the picture as Rāhu. Dharma and affection hemmed in her judgment, leaving her in the proverbial plight of the snake that has seized a shrew. If she asked her son to remain, dharma would be lost and strife with his kin would follow; if she told him to go, the harm would be immense. Overcome by this crisis, she reflected anew on a wife's duty and wisely regarded Rāma and Bharata alike as sons. Rāma's guileless mother gathered deep courage and said that he had done well, for a father's command is the crown of every duty. The forest itself did not grieve her; without him, however, Bharata, the king, and the subjects would suffer crushing pain.

Kausalyā said that if the command came only from his father, Rāma should regard her as the senior mother and not go; but if father and mother both had told him to leave, the forest equaled a hundred Ayodhyās. There the forest god would be his father, the forest goddess his mother, and birds and beasts would serve his lotus feet. Even at the end of life forest exile was hardly fitting for the king, and the thought of his age made her heart ache. Blessed was the forest and unfortunate Ayodhyā, which was losing the jewel of Raghu's line. If he asked her to accompany him, she feared that this might trouble his heart; he was dearer than life to everyone, yet told his mother to remain while he went away. She would not press a false show of love, but begged him, by the bond of motherhood, never to let remembrance of her fade.

May all the gods and ancestors guard you, my lord, as eyelids guard the eyes, Kausalyā prayed. The appointed term is the water and your loved ones are the fish; compassionate champion of dharma, devise a way to return while all are still alive. Go safely to the forest, though by going you leave the people, family, and city orphaned. The fruit of everyone's merit seemed exhausted that day and hostile Time had turned dreadful. Lamenting in many ways, she clung to his feet and counted herself utterly unfortunate; the harsh, unbearable burning that filled her heart and the forms of her grief cannot be described. Rāma raised his mother, held her to his breast, and again consoled her gently. Just then Sītā heard the news, rose in distress, bowed to both lotus feet of her mother-in-law, and sat with lowered head.

Kausalyā softly blessed Sītā, but seeing the exceedingly delicate princess she grew anxious. Sītā, a treasury of beauty and pure in her love for her husband, sat with downcast face and brooded: the lord of her life meant to leave for the forest—what fortunate person would accompany him? Would body and life both remain, or life alone? Fate's design could not be known. Her charming toes traced the ground, and the sweet chime of her anklets seemed to the poet like a plea born of love: do not abandon us from Sītā's feet. Seeing tears fall from her lovely eyes, Rāma's mother told him that Sītā was most tender and dear to her parents-in-law and family. Her father was Janaka, jewel among kings; her father-in-law the sun of the solar line; her husband the moon that opens the water lilies of Raghu's race and the home of every virtue and beauty.

Kausalyā said she had received in Sītā a beloved daughter-in-law, a treasury of beauty, virtue, character, and grace. She had cherished her like the pupil of her eye and the life within her life, tending this wish-fulfilling vine with the water of affection in countless ways. Just as it began to flower and fruit, Fate turned hostile; no one could foresee the outcome. Sītā had left couch and stool only for the cradle of her lap, and Kausalyā had never allowed her foot to touch the hard earth. She had guarded her like a life-restoring herb and would not even ask her to move a lamp's wick. Now that same Sītā wished to go to the forest: what was Rāma's command? How could the moonbeam-loving cakora bird set its eyes toward the sun? A forest filled with fierce lions, demons, and many wicked creatures was a garden of poison, no place for this beautiful, living herb of life.

The forest was made for the simple daughters of Kol and Kirāta tribes, inexperienced in worldly comforts; like worms born in the soles of feet, they found no hardship there. It also suited ascetics' wives who had renounced every pleasure for austerity. But how could Sītā live there when even a painted monkey frightened her? Was the lovely lotus of the celestial river fit for a pond, or a young swan for scrubland? Kausalyā asked Rāma to decide as he thought proper, promising to give Jānakī the corresponding counsel. If Sītā remained at home, she would be a great support to her. Hearing his mother's loving words, steeped as though in the nectar of character and affection, Rāma answered with tender, discerning speech, satisfied her, and began to explain to Jānakī the forest's virtues and dangers.
